title: De Morgan's laws with a universal set
statements: $(A B)ᶜ = Aᶜ \cap Bᶜ. \cup$

tactical_explanations:
**A) $(A B)ᶜ = {9, 10}. \cup$**  (true)

**B) $(A B)ᶜ = Aᶜ \cap Bᶜ. \cup$**  (true)

This is De Morgan's law for sets, and it holds generally - the complement of a union equals the intersection of the complements.

The claim matches the computation above, so it is **true**.

**C) $(A \cap B)ᶜ = Aᶜ Bᶜ. \cup$**  (true)

This is the other De Morgan's law - the complement of an intersection equals the union of the complements - and it also holds generally.

The claim matches the computation above, so it is **true**.

**D) $A \cap B$ = ${4, 5, 6}$.**  (false)

$A \cap B$ consists of elements in both sets: only 4 and 5 qualify (6 is in B but not in A), so $A \cap B$ = ${4,5}$, not ${4,5,6}$.

This is a common trap; the corrected reading shows the claim is **false**.

**E) $(A \cap B)ᶜ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10}.$**  (false)

Since $A \cap B$ = ${4,5}$, its complement relative to U is everything else: ${1,2,3,6,7,8,9,10}$. The set given here wrongly includes 4 and 5 and wrongly omits 6, 7, and 8.

title: Customer survey overlap
context: Let A be the set of customers who like Product A, with |A| = 120. Let B be the set of customers who like Product B, with |B| = 90. It is found that |$A \cap B$| = 50 customers like both products.
statements: The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170.$\cup$
The number of customers who like neither product is 40.
The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.
$A \cap B$ A.$\subseteq$
Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170.$\cup$**  (false)

$Trap: by inclusion-exclusion, |A B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 120 + 90 - 50 = 160, not 170 - a \cup simple arithmetic slip.$

This is a common trap; the corrected reading shows the claim is **false**.

**B) The number of customers who like neither product is 40.**  (true)

Out of 200 surveyed customers, 160 like at least one product (part a), so 200 - 160 = 40 like neither.

The claim matches the computation above, so it is **true**.

**C) The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.**  (false)

$Trap: customers who like only Product A are those in A but excluded from the overlap: |A| - |A \cap B| = 120 - 50 = 70, not 90.$

This is a common trap; the corrected reading shows the claim is **false**.

**D) $A \cap B$ A.$\subseteq$**  (true)

Every customer who likes both products necessarily likes Product A, so by definition the intersection is always a subset of A (and, symmetrically, of B) - this holds for any two sets, not just this survey.

The claim matches the computation above, so it is **true**.

**E) Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.**  (false)

Trap: this only forces |$A \cap B$| ≥ |A| + |B| - 200 = 210 - 200 = 10, a MINIMUM bound, not an exact value. The actual overlap (50, as given) is consistent with, and comfortably exceeds, this minimum - "exactly 10" overreaches what the bound alone can prove. PART II - Logic Tier 1 - Foundations

This is a common trap; the corrected reading shows the claim is **false**.

Let A be the set of customers who like Product A, with |A| = 120. Let B be the set of customers who like Product B, with |B| = 90. It is found that |$A \cap B$| = 50 customers like both products.

**Part 1: Setup.**

By inclusion-exclusion: |A B| = |A|+|B|-|$A \cap B$| = 120+90-50 = 160, so 200-160=40 $like \cup neither$, and |A only| = |A|-|$A \cap B$| = 120-50=70. Separately, since |A B|≤200 always, the counts 120+90=210 $alone \cup force$ |$A \cap B$|≥210-200=10 as a guaranteed minimum - the actual value 50 comfortably exceeds this floor.

**Part 2: Key facts.**

Use the definitions of membership, subset, union, intersection, difference, complement, and power set as needed. Compute shared objects once.

**Part 3: Solve.**

**1.** (FALSE) The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170.$\cup$

$Trap: by inclusion-exclusion, |A B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B| = 120 + 90 - 50 = 160, not 170 - a \cup simple arithmetic slip.$

**2.** (TRUE) The number of customers who like neither product is 40.

Out of 200 surveyed customers, 160 like at least one product (part a), so 200 - 160 = 40 like neither.

**3.** (FALSE) The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.

$Trap: customers who like only Product A are those in A but excluded from the overlap: |A| - |A \cap B| = 120 - 50 = 70, not 90.$

**4.** (TRUE) $A \cap B$ A.$\subseteq$

Every customer who likes both products necessarily likes Product A, so by definition the intersection is always a subset of A (and, symmetrically, of B) - this holds for any two sets, not just this survey.

**5.** (FALSE) Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.

Trap: this only forces |$A \cap B$| ≥ |A| + |B| - 200 = 210 - 200 = 10, a MINIMUM bound, not an exact value. The actual overlap (50, as given) is consistent with, and comfortably exceeds, this minimum - "exactly 10" overreaches what the bound alone can prove. PART II - Logic Tier 1 - Foundations

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
